title: Balance Sheet Classification & Presentation
description: Apply CPA-level classification and presentation rules for assets, liabilities and equity.
html:
Purpose of the balance sheet

The balance sheet presents an entity's financial position at a specific date.

Assets = Liabilities + Stockholders' Equity

FAR questions may require you to determine not only the correct balance of an account, but also where and how that balance should appear in the financial statements.

CPA mindset

Always separate these two questions:

  1. What is the correct amount?
  2. How should that amount be classified and presented?

Classified balance sheet

A classified balance sheet separates assets and liabilities into meaningful categories, including current and noncurrent classifications.

Current Assets

Current assets generally include assets expected to be realized in cash, sold, or consumed during the normal operating cycle or within one year from the balance-sheet date, whichever period is longer, when applicable.

Noncurrent Assets

Assets not classified as current, such as many long-term investments, property and equipment and intangible assets.

Current assets

Common current assets can include:

  • Cash and cash equivalents
  • Short-term receivables
  • Inventory
  • Certain short-term investments
  • Prepaid expenses expected to be consumed in the current period

Operating cycle

The operating cycle is the time between acquiring goods or services and ultimately converting them into cash through normal operations.

This concept matters because some operating assets and liabilities can remain current even when their realization or settlement extends beyond exactly twelve months.

Example

Assume a business has a normal operating cycle of 15 months.

Inventory expected to be sold and collected within that normal operating cycle may still qualify as current even though the cycle exceeds one year.

CPA trap

Do not automatically use: "anything over 12 months = noncurrent."

The operating cycle can matter.

Noncurrent assets

Noncurrent assets commonly include:

  • Property, plant and equipment
  • Long-term investments
  • Intangible assets
  • Certain long-term receivables
  • Other assets not meeting current-asset classification

Current liabilities

Current liabilities generally include obligations expected to be settled during the normal operating cycle or within one year from the balance-sheet date, whichever period is longer, when applicable.

Common examples

  • Accounts payable
  • Accrued wages payable
  • Certain taxes payable
  • Unearned revenue expected to be earned in the current period
  • Current maturities of long-term debt

Current portion of long-term debt

Long-term debt can contain both a current and a noncurrent portion.

Example

A company reports a $500,000 long-term note payable.

Of that amount, $80,000 is due during the next year.

Ignoring any special classification issues:

Current Liability $80,000
Noncurrent Liability $420,000
$500,000 − $80,000 = $420,000 noncurrent

Working capital

Working capital measures the excess of current assets over current liabilities.

Working Capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities

Example

Current assets = $300,000

Current liabilities = $190,000

$300,000 − $190,000 = $110,000 Working Capital

Contra accounts

Some accounts reduce the carrying amount of another account rather than appearing as ordinary liabilities or expenses.

Accounts Receivable

$200,000

Allowance for Credit Losses

($12,000)

Net Accounts Receivable = $200,000 − $12,000 = $188,000

The allowance is a contra-asset account. It reduces the carrying amount of receivables.

CPA trap

A contra-asset is not automatically classified as a liability simply because it has a credit balance.

Accumulated depreciation

Accumulated depreciation is another common contra-asset account.

Equipment cost = $250,000

Accumulated depreciation = $70,000

Net Carrying Amount = $250,000 − $70,000 = $180,000

Stockholders' equity presentation

Stockholders' equity can include several components rather than one single account.

  • Common stock
  • Preferred stock, when applicable
  • Additional paid-in capital
  • Retained earnings
  • Accumulated other comprehensive income or loss
  • Treasury stock as a reduction of equity

CPA trap

Treasury stock is generally presented as a reduction of stockholders' equity.

It is not presented as an asset merely because the corporation paid cash to reacquire its own shares.

Offsetting

Assets and liabilities generally should not simply be netted against one another merely because doing so makes the balance sheet shorter.

Whether amounts may be offset depends on the applicable accounting guidance and the facts of the arrangement.

CPA habit

If a problem gives you both an asset and a liability, do not automatically subtract one from the other.

Worked CPA-style classification problem

Assume a company reports:

Cash $40,000
Accounts Receivable, net $70,000
Inventory $90,000
Prepaid Insurance $10,000
Equipment, net $200,000
Accounts Payable $55,000
Current Portion of Debt $25,000

Step 1 — Calculate current assets

$40,000 + $70,000 + $90,000 + $10,000 = $210,000

Step 2 — Calculate current liabilities

$55,000 + $25,000 = $80,000

Step 3 — Calculate working capital

$210,000 − $80,000 = $130,000

Equipment is excluded from current assets because it is a noncurrent asset.

What you should know after this lesson

  • Distinguish current and noncurrent assets and liabilities.
  • Understand the importance of the operating cycle.
  • Separate current maturities from long-term debt.
  • Calculate working capital.
  • Understand contra-asset presentation.
  • Recognize treasury stock as contra-equity.
  • Do not automatically offset assets and liabilities.

quiz.prompt: A company has $260,000 of current assets and $175,000 of current liabilities. A $40,000 portion of long-term debt due next year is already included in current liabilities. What is working capital?
quiz.explanation: Working capital equals current assets minus current liabilities. Because the $40,000 current portion of debt is already included in the $175,000 current-liability total, it must not be subtracted a second time. $260,000 − $175,000 = $85,000.

objectives: Explain balance sheet classification & presentation and its underlying principles.
Apply the topic to a financial-reporting scenario.
Evaluate common errors and their financial-statement effects.
